theory.intro: The equation $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=k(Q-P)$ is solved by $Q=P+Ae^{kt}$. To **verify** this, differentiate it and substitute back. Putting $t=0$ gives $A=Q(0)-P$, the initial difference.
facts: Differentiating gives $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kAe^{kt}$, and since $Ae^{kt}=Q-P$ this is $k(Q-P)$.
Checking only that $Q(0)$ comes out right is not a verification, because it never uses the derivative.
$A=Q(0)-P$, so $A$ is the initial difference and $P+A$ is the initial value.
If $A=0$ then $Q=P$ for every $t$, and the rate stays zero.
$A>0$ puts the whole curve above the line $Q=P$, and $A<0$ puts it below.
For $k>0$ and $A\ne0$ the size of $Ae^{kt}$ grows without bound as $t$ increases, so the curve moves away from $Q=P$.

When $A\ne0$, find $k$ by substituting a second pair of values at a different time and taking natural logarithms. The data must give a positive value of $e^{kt}$, so the second difference $Q-P$ must be nonzero and have the same sign as $A$. If $A=0$ and both observations equal $P$, $k$ cannot be determined; a second observation different from $P$ is incompatible with the model.
steps: Differentiate the proposed function to find $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}$.
Substitute $t=0$ to find $A$. If $A\ne0$, use a compatible second pair of values at a different time to find $k$; if $A=0$ and both observations equal $P$, $k$ cannot be determined.

Sketch through $(0,\,P+A)$. For $k<0$ and $A\ne0$, sketch a curve approaching the horizontal asymptote $Q=P$; for $k>0$ and $A\ne0$, sketch a curve moving away from $Q=P$ for $t\ge0$. For $A=0$, sketch the constant line $Q=P$; for $k=0$, sketch the constant line $Q=P+A$.

workedExamples.question_text:
Verify by differentiation and substitution that each function satisfies its differential equation.
(a) $Q=28+36e^{kt}$; $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=k(Q-28)$.
(b) $N=900-300e^{-kt}$; $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=-k(N-900)$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Differentiate the proposed function:
$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}&=36ke^{kt}.\end{aligned}$
Substitute into the right-hand side:
$\begin{aligned}k(Q-28)&=k(28+36e^{kt}-28)\\&=36ke^{kt}.\end{aligned}$
Both sides agree, so the function satisfies the differential equation.
(b) Differentiate the proposed function:
$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dN}{dt}&=(-300)(-k)e^{-kt}\\&=300ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}$
Substitute into the right-hand side:
$\begin{aligned}-k(N-900)&=-k(900-300e^{-kt}-900)\\&=300ke^{-kt}.\end{aligned}$
Both sides agree. The negative coefficient and negative exponent produce a positive derivative when $k>0$.

workedExamples.question_text:
A drink cools in a room at $22^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Its temperature is modelled by $T=22+Ae^{kt}$, where $t$ is measured in minutes. Initially its temperature is $86^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, and after $6$ minutes it is $54^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
(a) Find $A$ and $k$ in exact form.
(b) Find its temperature after $12$ minutes.
(c) Sketch the temperature against time for $t\ge0$, showing the initial temperature and horizontal asymptote.

A battery charges towards a maximum charge of $100\%$. Initially its charge is $20\%$, and after $4$ minutes it is $60\%$. Its charge is modelled by $Q=P+Ae^{kt}$, where $k<0$ and $t$ is measured in minutes.
(a) Write an expression for $Q(t)$ before determining $k$.
(b) Find $k$ in exact form.
(c) Sketch $Q$ against $t$ for $t\ge0$, labelling the initial charge and asymptote.

Sketch each function for $t\ge0$, showing its initial value and the line $Q=30$. Describe whether it has a limiting value.
(a) $Q=30+10e^{0.2t}$.
(b) $Q=30-10e^{0.2t}$.

The graph of $Q=8+Ae^{kt}$ passes through $(0,12)$ and $(3,40)$.
Find $A$ and $k$ in exact form. State whether the graph approaches a limiting value as $t\to\infty$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Use the initial point:
$\begin{aligned}12&=8+A\\A&=4.\end{aligned}$
Use the second point:
$\begin{aligned}40&=8+4e^{3k}\\32&=4e^{3k}\\e^{3k}&=8\\3k&=\ln8\\k&=\ln2.\end{aligned}$
Thus $Q=8+4e^{(\ln2)t}$. Since $A>0$ and $k>0$, the curve rises away from $Q=8$ and grows without bound. It has no finite limiting value.

foundation.solution_text:
$T=30+45e^{kt}$
$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=45ke^{kt}$
Also $T-30=45e^{kt}$, so $k(T-30)=45ke^{kt}$.
Both sides equal $45ke^{kt}$, so $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=k(T-30)$.

$N=1200-700e^{kt}$
$\dfrac{dN}{dt}=-700ke^{kt}$
Also $N-1200=-700e^{kt}$, so $k(N-1200)=-700ke^{kt}$.
Both sides equal $-700ke^{kt}$, so $\dfrac{dN}{dt}=k(N-1200)$.

development.question_text:
A quantity is modelled by $N=800-500e^{kt}$, and $N=500$ when $t=4$.
Find $k$ in exact form.

development.solution_text:
$Q=60+20e^{kt}$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=20ke^{kt}$
Also $Q-60=20e^{kt}$, so $k(Q-60)=20ke^{kt}$.
Both sides equal $20ke^{kt}$, so $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=k(Q-60)$.

$Q=50-12e^{-kt}$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=12ke^{-kt}$
Also $Q-50=-12e^{-kt}$, so $-k(Q-50)=-k(-12e^{-kt})=12ke^{-kt}$.
Both sides equal $12ke^{-kt}$, so $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-k(Q-50)$.

development.question_text:
The mass of salt in a tank is modelled by $S=15+Ae^{kt}$ kg.
Initially $S=3$, and $S=9$ after $5$ hours.
Find $A$ and $k$ in exact form.
Sketch $N=500+200e^{0.15t}$ for $t\ge 0$, showing the value at $t=0$ and the line $N=500$.

A phone battery has an initial charge of $12\%$ and charges towards a maximum of $40\%$. Its charge $Q$ is modelled by $Q=P+Ae^{kt}$, where $k<0$.
Write an expression for $Q(t)$ and draw a quick sketch for $t\ge0$.
development.solution_text:
$P=40$
$12=40+A$
$A=-28$
So $Q(t)=40-28e^{kt}$, where $k<0$.
The curve starts at $(0,12)$ and rises towards the horizontal asymptote $Q=40$, becoming less steep as $t$ increases.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$t$}, ylabel={$Q$}, xmin=-0.5, xmax=10.6, ymin=-5, ymax=48, samples=100, clip=false, ytick={12,40}, xtick=\empty]
\addplot[dashed, domain=0:10.6] (x,40);
\addplot[smooth, thick, ->, domain=0:10] {40-28*exp(-0.4*x)};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
The sketch shows the shape for $k<0$; no particular value of $k$ is given.

$T=18-26e^{-kt}$
$\dfrac{dT}{dt}=26ke^{-kt}$
Also $T-18=-26e^{-kt}$, so $-k(T-18)=-k\left(-26e^{-kt}\right)=26ke^{-kt}$.
Both sides equal $26ke^{-kt}$, so $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-18)$.

mastery.question_text:
A quantity is modelled by $Q=45+Ae^{kt}$, with $Q=85$ when $t=0$ and $Q=65$ when $t=10$.
Find $A$ and $k$ in exact form, then find $Q$ when $t=20$.

mastery.solution_text:
$Q=70-25e^{-kt}$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=25ke^{-kt}$
Also $Q-70=-25e^{-kt}$, so $-k(Q-70)=-k(-25e^{-kt})=25ke^{-kt}$.
Both sides equal $25ke^{-kt}$, so $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-k(Q-70)$.

mastery.question_text:
The graph of $Q=6+Ae^{kt}$ passes through $(0,\,9)$ and $(2,\,18)$, and bends away from the line $Q=6$.
Find $A$ and $k$ in exact form, and state whether $Q$ has a limiting value.
mastery.solution_text:
$9=6+A$
$A=3$
$18=6+3e^{2k}$
$12=3e^{2k}$
$e^{2k}=4$
$2k=\ln 4$
$k=\ln 2$
Since $k>0$ the term $3e^{kt}$ grows without bound, so $Q$ has no limiting value.
